newsitem.title: USA: Clinton plan to keep Medicare solvent until 2007.
newsitem.headline: Clinton plan to keep Medicare solvent until 2007.

text.p: President Clinton's plan to reduce Medicare spending by $138 billion over six years will ensure the solvency of the federal health program through early 2007, administration officials said Wednesday.

In a memo, the chief actuary of the government Health Care Financing Administration estimated the White House proposal would extend the life of Medicare's Part A hospital trust fund, now estimated to go broke in 2001, for six years.
Clinton outlined his proposal Tuesday, saying he wanted to meet Republicans halfway on balancing the budget. It will be formally submitted to Congress next month.
"These are scorable savings. There are no gimmicks and this package, as the president indicated, does meet the Republcians halfway," Health Secretary Donna Shalala told reporters Wednesday.

The White House pounded Republicans in November elections, saying their failed 1995 plan for $270 billion in Medicare reductions would have devastated the program. The new White House proposal gets most of its savings from cuts to health care providers. The plan avoids big increases in Medicare premiums and actually expands benefits.

While Shalala said the plan did not contain any gimmicks, it does include a proposal to shift part of the cost of Medicare's home health program, more than $50 billion, out of the Part A hospital trust fund.

By transferring the spending out of Part A, the change will make the hospital trust fund appear more robust, extending its shelf life. The administration plans separate spending reductions in home health to help balance the budget.
Some Republicans have derided the home health transfer as a gimmick, saying the White House is using it to avoid making more painful cuts needed to ensure the solvency of Medicare.

The proposal would provide new benefits for preventive care including colorectal screening, diabetes management and annual mammograms without copayments. It would give senior citizens more latitute to choose alternative care plans.

It would also ensure that senior citizens paid no more than a 20 percent copayment for hospital outpatient services. Due to glitches in current Medicare rules, seniors can end up paying an effective copayment of as much as 50 percent.
The plan would reduce Medicare reduce hospital payments by about $45 billion over six years and cut managed care reimbursement by $46 billion.
